saccharomyces-ferment.text: Users of K-beauty essences, especially SK-II's Pitera, apply yeast ferment filtrate in pursuit of smoother, more radiant skin. Its fame comes largely from brand storytelling, and direct trials of the ingredient on appearance are almost absent.

kombucha-ferment.text: Kombucha ferment is used in serums and toners as an antioxidant, calming botanical aimed at fresher-looking skin. The evidence for skin appearance consists of lab-dish antioxidant data; human skin trials are untested.

tremella-mushroom.text: Tremella, or snow fungus, is used in Asian skincare as a plant alternative to hyaluronic acid, promoted to hydrate skin and soften the look of fine lines. Support for that use comes from patents and brand claims rather than human trials.

mugwort.text: Mugwort extract is a staple of K-beauty toners and masks, used by people with reactive skin who want a calmer, less red complexion. Its folk use is long, while trials of its effect on skin appearance are absent.

houttuynia-cordata.text: Heartleaf extract appears in Korean toners, serums and sheet masks used for calming redness and oily, blemish-prone skin. Cell-culture data on inflammation exist, while human skin-appearance trials are essentially absent.

ginseng-root-extract.text: Ginseng root extract is used in K-beauty and herbal skincare, promoted as an antioxidant that gives skin a healthier, more youthful look. Its topical effect on appearance has not been tested in trials.

portulaca-oleracea.text: Purslane extract appears in soothing essences and moisturisers, where users reach for it to calm irritated skin and improve its look. Support consists of lab and animal data; skin-appearance trials in people are untested.

scutellaria-baicalensis-root-extract.text: Baikal skullcap root extract is used in cosmetics as an anti-inflammatory or brightening botanical, aimed at redness and uneven tone. Small human trials are registered, but little has been published on its effect on skin appearance.

perilla-seed-extract.text: Perilla seed extract is included in some cosmetics as a plant-based omega-3 and antioxidant ingredient, promoted for softer, healthier-looking skin. Human studies of its appearance effects have not been done.

camellia-japonica-extract.text: Japanese camellia extract is used in some cosmetics, with Korean patent filings describing it for anti-ageing, whitening and anti-inflammatory purposes. Evidence for that use is limited to a mouse study; human data are untested.

hemp-seed-oil.text: Hemp seed oil is used in moisturisers and body care by people wanting soft, well-hydrated skin, and is often chosen for its high linoleic acid content. Skin-specific trials are few, so its appearance benefits rest mostly on general emollient reasoning.

volcanic-ash.text: Volcanic ash appears in some K-beauty masks and cleansers, promoted to absorb oil and leave oily skin looking matte. The sources found describe the geology of ash, and trials of any skin benefit are untested.

witch-hazel-extract.text: Witch hazel is a classic astringent toner used by people with oily or blemish-prone skin to reduce shine and give a tighter feel. Lab data on its properties exist, while human skin trials are lacking.

pine-bark-extract.text: Maritime pine bark extract (Pycnogenol) is taken or applied as an antioxidant in anti-aging and skin-brightening routines. It has been studied for many conditions, but its appearance effects are not the main focus of that research.

mistletoe-extract.text: Mistletoe extract appears as a botanical in some Korean-style skincare products, where it is promoted for soothing and general skin health. Its research is in complementary cancer care rather than skin, so the appearance link is untested.

noni-fruit-extract.text: Noni extract is sold as juice, supplements and cosmetics, promoted as an antioxidant for a brighter, more youthful complexion. Evidence for skin appearance is lab-only.

moringa.text: Moringa seed oil and leaf extract are used in skin and hair products as a light moisturiser and antioxidant for smoother, healthier-looking skin. Antioxidant lab data exist, while skin-appearance trials are untested.

yuzu-extract.text: Yuzu extract is used in Asian skincare as a vitamin C botanical, promoted for brightening and evening out skin tone. Lab antioxidant and pigment data exist, and skin trials are untested.

horse-oil.text: Horse oil (ma-yu) is used in Japanese and Korean creams as a rich emollient, chosen because its fatty acids resemble human skin lipids. Support comes from small formulation and cell studies, with human appearance trials untested.

starfish-extract.text: Starfish extract is a K-beauty marine ingredient promoted for moisturising and regenerating skin, inspired by starfish regrowing lost arms. Support is limited to a zebrafish study and patents; human effects are untested.

pig-collagen.text: Pig collagen appears in Korean sheet masks and creams for plumper, smoother skin, and is also taken as a supplement. Porcine collagen has real surgical uses, but cosmetic trials are lacking.

tea-tree-extract.text: Tea tree oil and extract are used in cleansers and spot treatments by people targeting acne and blemishes. The oil has limited acne trial evidence, while the extract has almost none.

acerola-fruit-extract.text: Acerola extract is included in beauty supplements as a natural vitamin C source, taken for brighter, firmer skin. Skin evidence exists only for multi-ingredient blends, not for the extract on its own.

orchid-extract.text: Orchid extracts from species such as Dendrobium and Phalaenopsis are used in Asian skincare, promoted as antioxidant and anti-aging botanicals. Support is limited to lab, animal and patent material.

lotus-extract.text: Sacred lotus extract is used in K-beauty skincare as an antioxidant botanical for a calmer, brighter complexion. Only two small human studies exist, both pairing it with green tea.

green-tea-camellia-sinensis-leaf-extract.text: Green tea extract is a common skincare antioxidant, also taken orally, used by people aiming for calmer, more youthful skin and fewer breakouts. It is widely studied for general health, with appearance-specific support more limited.

papaya-extract.text: Papaya extract is used as an enzyme exfoliant in masks and cleansers, promoted for smoother, brighter skin through papain's protein-digesting action. Skin-appearance trials for the extract were not found.

oat-extract.text: Colloidal oat and oat extracts are used in sensitive-skin, baby and sun-care products to calm dry, irritated skin. Colloidal oatmeal holds FDA skin-protectant status, while trials of oat extracts for appearance are mostly dietary.

cucumber-extract.text: Cucumber extract is a cooling botanical in cleansers, gels and eye products, used for a fresh feel and a less puffy, tired-looking eye area. It is included more for mild hydration than as an active ingredient, with no controlled appearance trials.

chamomile-extract.text: Chamomile extract is a common soothing ingredient in creams, cleansers and masks, used by people with sensitive or red skin for a calmer look. Lab data on inflammation and oral-use trials exist, while skin-appearance trials do not.
